narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically denied your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors in your profile. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. It sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted, signaling weaker academic preparation in the eyes of the model. Your LSAT score of 37 was the second most important factor and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction slightly toward passing; it is almost identical to the average of accepted students. Your class rank at the end of your third year (decile 3) came in third. At 5.00 it is very close to the 5.79 average of accepted students, yet it still nudged the outcome slightly toward failure.

Taken together, the below-average college grades outweighed the solid LSAT and typical class rank, producing a failure probability high enough to trigger rejection. Gender, race, family income bracket, and full-time status played no role in this outcome.

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen your academic record before reapplying. Retake challenging courses to raise your GPA, consider a post-baccalaureate program, or enroll in a master’s degree that demonstrates sustained high performance. A higher GPA will directly counteract the element that hurt your application most.
